intro: In February 1632 a Florentine press finished printing Galileo's Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems, a conversation in Italian among three friends weighing Ptolemy against Copernicus. It carried the licence of the Master of the Sacred Palace in Rome and the Florentine inquisitor. By late summer it was impounded. In September Pope Urban VIII, who as Cardinal Maffeo Barberini had been Galileo's admirer, sent the case to the Congregation of the Holy Office. Ten months later, on 22 June 1633, Galileo knelt in the Dominican convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, heard himself declared 'vehemently suspect of heresy', and abjured. This is a trial built from letters and from the court's own file, not from diaries. The Holy Office kept minutes, depositions taken down by a notary in Latin and Italian, consultors' reports, a papal decision and the sentence; the file stayed in the Vatican and was published in full only in the nineteenth century, with modern critical editions since. Beside it run the dispatches of Francesco Niccolini, the Tuscan ambassador who housed Galileo, which are the main source for what Urban VIII said in private audiences. The Pope's words reach us only through Niccolini's reports, and the form tags say so. Galileo's own letters, and the weekly letters of his daughter Suor Maria Celeste from her convent at Arcetri, give the view from the accused's family. Most of these texts are in Italian and appear here as paraphrase, drawn from Antonio Favaro's Edizione Nazionale (1890–1909); short quotations come only from English translations published before 1929. The legal heart of the case was a single sheet. In the 1616 file was an unsigned minute stating that on 26 February 1616 the Commissary of the Holy Office, in Cardinal Bellarmine's presence, had ordered Galileo not to hold, teach or defend Copernicus's opinion 'in any way whatever'. Galileo held a certificate from Bellarmine, dated 26 May 1616, saying only that he had been told of the general decree. Whether that minute records what was actually said, and why it is unsigned, has been argued over since it came to light. Historians remain divided, and the chapter sets the documents side by side rather than deciding. Around the court stand the people who wrote while the case went on: the Commissary Vincenzo Maculano, who talked Galileo into a plea in a private session and reported it to the Cardinal-nephew Francesco Barberini; Benedetto Castelli, Galileo's former pupil; Archbishop Ascanio Piccolomini of Siena, who took the condemned man into his palace; the Servite Fulgenzio Micanzio in Venice; and, abroad, Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc in Provence and René Descartes in the Netherlands, who hid his own treatise on the world when the news reached him. Behind them the plague of 1630–33 shut roads, put Galileo in quarantine on the Tuscan border and filled Maria Celeste's letters with remedies and deaths. Two famous elements are absent or flagged. The words 'Eppur si muove' ('and yet it moves'), supposedly muttered after the abjuration, appear in no record of 1633. They first appear in print in Giuseppe Baretti's Italian Library (London, 1757), and on a Spanish painting of Galileo in prison whose date and attribution are uncertain; they are a legend. The chapter ends with the dated facts of afterward: Galileo confined at Arcetri, Peiresc's plea of December 1634, and Pope John Paul II's address of 31 October 1992 to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences. That address was widely reported as a rehabilitation but was not a formal annulment of the 1633 sentence.

intro: Between December 1648 and March 1649 England did something no European state had done: it put its reigning king on trial in the name of the people, condemned him, cut off his head in front of his own palace, and abolished the monarchy. On 6 December Colonel Thomas Pride's soldiers stood at the door of the Commons and turned away or arrested the members who still wanted a settlement with the King. The remnant — the Rump — named a committee, declared itself the supreme power, and on 6 January passed an Act erecting a High Court of Justice of some 135 commissioners. The court sat in public in Westminster Hall on 20, 22, 23 and 27 January. Charles never pleaded. He denied that any power on earth could try him, and the trial became a series of confrontations between a prisoner who would not recognise the court and a Lord President, John Bradshaw, who would not let him argue the point. Because there was no plea, the witnesses were heard in private, and the Solicitor, John Cook, never made his speech — he printed it afterwards. The King was sentenced on 27 January, the warrant is dated the 29th, and he died on the afternoon of Tuesday 30 January. Almost everything said in the Hall comes from the court's side. The clerks' minute journal, printed in 1684 by a royalist editor, and the licensed day-by-day 'Perfect Narrative' pamphlets give the King's words faithfully enough to make his case, but they were made by the regime that was trying him. The scaffold speech was taken down in shorthand and printed 'by special authority'. Some of the most famous moments — Lady Fairfax's cries from the gallery, the King's last morning, the crowd's groan — survive only in accounts written later, sometimes decades later and under a restored monarchy, and are flagged here as such. Around that record stand the outside voices. A country vicar in Essex hears the news late and uncertain; a royalist virtuoso in Deptford hears a preacher urge the judges on, then stays home fasting; a thirteen-year-old princess writes down what her father told her; a schoolboy in the crowd remembers a sound; another schoolboy, grown into a naval official, is afraid in 1660 of the words he said that day. From Münster, where the Thirty Years War had just been ended, a Venetian diplomat follows the Dutch attempt to save the King and records Europe's verdict on its outcome. This chapter is built mostly from court minutes, parliamentary journals, licensed pamphlets, dated letters and later memoirs rather than diaries, and says so for each voice. It offers no verdict on whether the trial was justice or murder; it lays the accusers, the accused and the onlookers side by side, on the dates they wrote.

intro: In the winter of 1691–92 two girls in the household of Samuel Parris, minister of Salem Village in Massachusetts, began to suffer fits that a local doctor could not explain except as the work of an evil hand. By 1 March three women had been named and brought before two Salem magistrates: Sarah Good, Sarah Osborne, and Tituba, an enslaved woman in Parris's house. Tituba confessed. Over the next year more than 150 people from two dozen towns were jailed. A special Court of Oyer and Terminer, set up by the new royal governor in May, condemned more than two dozen; nineteen were hanged between June and September, Giles Corey was pressed to death for refusing to plead, and at least five died in jail. This chapter is built mostly from records rather than diaries. The court's own papers (warrants, examinations, depositions, petitions, indictments) survive in large numbers, and they are the nearest thing to the voices of the accused. But each examination was written down by a minister, magistrate or clerk who believed in the accusations and chose what to record, and many depositions were drafted later, in other hands, for trial. The papers are transcribed in the 1938 Works Progress Administration typescript, now on the University of Virginia archive, and in Rosenthal's Records of the Salem Witch-Hunt (2009). The form tags say which is which. Beside the court stand the accused who wrote: Rebecca Nurse, whose answers, petition and declaration are those of a half-deaf woman of seventy; her sister Mary Easty, whose last petition asked nothing for herself; John Proctor, writing from prison to the Boston ministers. The accusers appear through Ann Putnam Jr, twelve in 1692, whose depositions are mostly in her father's hand and whose confession of 1706 is her own. In between are the jury foreman Thomas Fisk, the minister Parris, and the visiting minister Deodat Lawson, whose day-by-day narrative of March is the only eyewitness account of the early examinations. Further off are the men who shaped and then ended the court: Samuel Sewall, the only judge who kept a diary and the only one who apologised; Cotton Mather, who advised caution in private and wrote the public defence; his father Increase, whose Cases of Conscience of October 1692 turned opinion; Thomas Brattle, a merchant whose private letter took the methods apart; and Governor Phips, whose reports to London show him stepping back from what he had started. Robert Calef, a Boston merchant who was not at the trials, collected the documents and the stories that became the most quoted scenes of 1692. His book is hostile to the Mathers, and the scenes that rest on his word alone are marked as his. The chapter does not try the case again. It records the dated reversals: Sewall's confession and the jurors' declaration in January 1697, Ann Putnam's confession in 1706, and the act of 17 October 1711 that declared twenty-two of the convictions null and void. The remaining names were cleared by Massachusetts in 1957, 2001 and, for the last, Elizabeth Johnson Jr, in 2022. Executions are described as the records describe them: who, when, and what the watchers wrote.

intro: On 13 February 1788 the peers of Great Britain filed into Westminster Hall to try Warren Hastings, Governor-General of Bengal from 1773 to 1785, on articles of impeachment brought by the House of Commons. The galleries held ladies, foreign envoys and writers who had queued from dawn; the managers' box held Edmund Burke, Charles James Fox, Richard Brinsley Sheridan, William Windham and Charles Grey. The trial sat for 145 days spread over seven years and three months. On 23 April 1795 Hastings was acquitted on every article, and he was left owing for a defence that, by his own reckoning, had cost him about £70,000. The charges looked back across a decade of Indian government. In 1775 Maharaja Nandakumar, who had accused Hastings of taking bribes, was convicted of forgery by the new Supreme Court at Calcutta and hanged. In August 1781 Hastings went to Benares to press Raja Chait Singh for arrears of a war subsidy and for cavalry, placed him under arrest, and had to withdraw to the fort at Chunar when the Raja's people rose. Early in 1782 the treasure and estates of the Begums of Oudh, the mother and grandmother of the Nawab Wazir, were seized at Faizabad by the Nawab's officers with Company backing. Prosecution and defence agreed on most of these facts. They disagreed about whether they were crimes, emergencies of war, or acts of Indian rulers for which Hastings was not answerable. The record is mostly speeches, the court's own printed minutes, letters and one great diary, rather than many diaries. The speeches survive in shorthand reports and in versions the speakers or their editors later revised, so the most famous lines are flagged as printed texts rather than verbatim transcripts. Fanny Burney, Keeper of the Robes to Queen Charlotte, attended on royal tickets, argued with the managers in the galleries, and wrote it all down as a declared partisan of Hastings. Edward Gibbon heard Sheridan praise his 'luminous page' and wrote about it later in his memoirs. Elizabeth Sheridan wrote to her sister-in-law of her husband's triumph. The Freemasons' Magazine timed the final sitting. The Indian side is harder to hear, and the chapter says so. Raja Chait Singh's reply to Hastings's charges of August 1781 survives because Hastings printed it in his own Narrative. The Begums appear only through depositions and the managers' speeches. The addresses sent from Benares, Lucknow and Bengal in Hastings's favour were attacked by Burke as manufactured and defended by Hastings's friends as spontaneous. Ghulam Husain Khan's Persian history, the Siyar al-Muta'akhkhirin, finished in 1781, judged English rule harshly from Patna. Its English translator, a French convert who signed himself Nota Manus and had served in Hastings's secretariat, praised the Governor-General in print in 1789. These voices disagree among themselves as much as the managers and counsel did. The chapter gives no verdict. The Lords acquitted, and only a few of the twenty-nine peers who voted found against Hastings on Benares and the Begums. Historians since have read the trial as a corrupt pursuit by party, as a founding statement that power in India answered to law, or as both.

intro: On 5 June 1820 Caroline of Brunswick landed at Dover to claim her place as Queen. Her husband, newly King George IV, had lived apart from her for almost twenty-five years and wanted her neither crowned nor prayed for. The next day he sent Parliament two green bags of evidence gathered by a commission in Milan, and by July Lord Liverpool's reluctant government had brought in a Bill of Pains and Penalties to strip her of her title and dissolve the marriage by Act of Parliament. It was not formally a trial, and that was the Queen's first complaint. But from 17 August to 10 November the House of Lords sat as a court: the Crown's law officers called Italian servants to swear to her adultery with her chamberlain Bartolomeo Pergami, and her counsel, Henry Brougham and Thomas Denman, cross-examined, called their own witnesses and summed up. The peers then voted, and when the third reading passed by only nine the government let the bill die. Eight months later she was turned away from the coronation; three weeks after that she was dead. The court's own record is here first: the Lords' Minutes of Evidence and Hansard's reports, close to verbatim for the witnesses, reported for the speeches. Beside it stand the people who wrote the case down as it happened. Caroline's own voice survives mostly in letters that others drafted, notably the open letter of 7 August 1820 generally credited to Cobbett, and in last words reported by Brougham. The King's survives in a formal message and in private letters. The witness Majocchi speaks only through interpreters, yet his 'non mi ricordo' became the most quoted phrase of the year. Outside the chamber, the Whig Thomas Creevey wrote to his stepdaughter almost daily from the gallery; the courtier Charles Greville kept his diary; W. H. Fremantle reported to the Marquess of Buckingham from beside the King's lodge at Windsor; Robert Plumer Ward kept a government man's diary; Harriet Arbuthnot heard from Wellington what passed in Cabinet; and Princess Lieven wrote to Metternich from the King's Pavilion at Brighton. The radical press, Cobbett's Register and William Hone's pamphlets, turned the evidence into weekly argument and cheap satire for a crowd that marched in its tens of thousands and signed addresses in numbers never seen before. The honest record is therefore mostly letters, an official transcript and printed pamphlets, with a few diaries. Every one of these writers took a side, and the question the Lords were asked, whether the Queen had committed adultery, was never decided: the bill was abandoned, not voted down on the evidence. This chapter sets out what each side said and recorded, and leaves that question where the House of Lords left it.

intro: Before dawn on 2 July 1839, off the north coast of Cuba, fifty-three Africans held on the Spanish schooner Amistad broke free and took the ship. The captain and the cook were killed and two sailors escaped in a boat. Two Cuban buyers, José Ruiz and Pedro Montes, were spared to sail the ship east to Africa. For eight weeks Montes steered east by day and north-west by night. On 26 August 1839 a US Navy survey brig, the Washington, found the schooner anchored off Culloden Point at the eastern end of Long Island and took it into New London, Connecticut. What followed was not one trial but a chain of them. There was a hearing on the deck of a warship, a grand jury and habeas corpus hearing in Hartford, and suits for false imprisonment in New York. A district-court trial in New Haven in January 1840 was followed by a pro forma appeal and then eight days of argument before the Supreme Court in Washington in February and March 1841. On every side were claims of property: the naval officers claimed salvage, the Cuban buyers wanted their 'slaves' back, and the Spanish government invoked a treaty. The Van Buren administration kept a navy schooner waiting in New Haven harbour in case the verdict went against the Africans. The chapter gives priority to the captives' own voices. Almost everything they said reached the record through an interpreter. For the first five weeks there was none who spoke Mende, until the Yale philologist Josiah Gibbs found James Covey, a young sailor on a British warship who had himself been freed from a slave ship. Sengbe Pieh (called Cinqué by the Americans), Grabeau and Fuliwa told their story through Covey in depositions and in court, and newspapers and Barber's 1840 pamphlet printed it in shortened and edited English. By January 1841 Kale and Kinna, two of the younger men, were writing letters in their own new English to John Quincy Adams. Each entry says whether the words passed through someone else. Few of these sources are diaries. The exceptions are John Quincy Adams's daily journal and, more briefly, Lewis Tappan's. The rest are court records (libels, decrees and the Supreme Court's opinion), an executive order, diplomatic notes, newspaper reports and dated letters, and the form tags say so. Some famous lines have doubtful origins. The most quoted words attributed to Cinqué, printed in New York before any interpreter had been found, are one example. The story told a century later, that he became a slave trader after going home, is another. Historians have traced it to a 1946 book and found no evidence for it. The courts did not decide whether the revolt was justified as a moral question. The Supreme Court held on 9 March 1841 that the Africans had been kidnapped and illegally imported into Cuba and were not property under Spanish law, so they were free. It also overturned the lower court's order handing them to the President for removal, so they were simply released. No public money paid for their passage home. Thirty-five survivors sailed from New York in late November 1841 with missionaries and reached Sierra Leone in January 1842.

intro: On the night of Sunday 16 October 1859 John Brown led twenty-one men into Harpers Ferry, Virginia, and seized the federal armory, meaning to arm enslaved people and start a war on slavery from the mountains. Thirty-six hours later Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee broke into the engine house where he had made his stand. Ten raiders were dead, two of them his sons, along with four men of the town and district, among them the free Black baggage master Heyward Shepherd, and one Marine. Brown, wounded, was questioned on the floor of the paymaster's office by a senator, a congressman and a crowd of reporters. What followed was a trial that both sides treated as a stage. Virginia tried Brown in its own county court at Charles Town, not in a federal court, and moved fast: indictment on 26 October, verdict on 31 October, sentence on 2 November, hanging on 2 December. His men followed him to the gallows on 16 December and 16 March. In the meantime Brown wrote letter after letter from his cell, and newspapers North and South printed them, along with his interview and his speech before sentence. The record here is mixed and the form tags say so. The court's formal papers survive, but the proceedings are known mainly from reporters' shorthand and from pamphlets put together by one side or the other. Brown's own words come through those reporters and through his manuscript letters. Around them stand an official US Army report, a governor's papers, letters between strangers that were printed as a pamphlet, public lectures, a soldier's letter, a secessionist's diary, two condemned men's letters, a raider's memoir written later, and a Senate report with two opposed conclusions. The eyes divide sharply. Lee called the plan the work of a fanatic or madman; Governor Wise called its leader brave and truthful and then refused him mercy; Senator Mason and his wife saw Northern money and the threat of a slave rising. Thoreau in Concord and Lydia Maria Child in Wayland, saw a man of principle; Frederick Douglass, named in the captured papers, wrote from Canada to deny that he had promised to come. Osborne Anderson, who escaped, and John Copeland, who did not, are the two Black raiders whose words survive. Victor Hugo's plea from Guernsey was written on the day of the hanging. This chapter gives no verdict on the raid or the trial. It sets out what each side wrote, and it records the deaths, of raiders, townspeople and a Marine, without dwelling on them. The epilogue is the Senate's inquiry under Mason, which heard the same testimony and returned two reports: one blaming Northern backers, one saying the free states had no part in it.

intro: In late September 1894 a torn, unsigned list of military documents offered to the German military attaché reached the French army's intelligence section. Within three weeks Captain Alfred Dreyfus, an Alsatian Jewish artillery officer on the General Staff, had been made to write a dictated letter, judged to have a hand like the list's, and locked in the Cherche-Midi prison. A court-martial sitting behind closed doors convicted him in December; in January he was publicly stripped of his rank, and by April he was alone on Devil's Island off French Guiana. The case did not end there, and the chapter follows it to its legal end: the discovery in 1896 that another officer's handwriting matched the list; that officer's acquittal in January 1898; Zola's 'J'accuse…!' two days later and his own conviction for libel; the exposure of a forged document and the forger's death in August 1898; the annulment of the 1894 verdict in June 1899; a second court-martial at Rennes that convicted again 'with extenuating circumstances'; a presidential pardon eleven days later; and the Cour de cassation's annulment of the Rennes judgment on 12 July 1906. The record is uneven, and the chapter says so. The 1894 trial left no transcript; what was said in that room comes from later inquiries. The Zola trial and the Rennes court-martial, by contrast, were taken down in shorthand and printed. Dreyfus's own voice survives in letters that officials read before delivery and in the diary he kept on Devil's Island; Zola's in articles he collected himself. Several voices are memoirs or journals published decades later — Blum's 'Souvenirs' (1935), Paléologue's journal (1955), Mathieu Dreyfus's memoir (1978) — and are marked as such and given only in outline. The accusers are here in their own documents too: La Libre Parole, which named the prisoner before the army did and campaigned against him as a Jew; Major Henry's testimony and his forgery; Esterhazy's acquittal and his later claims to the English press. They are reported as what they said and did, without the slurs. Abroad, a Viennese correspondent, an English reporter, an American wire service, a London weekly and an American novelist in Paris show how far the case travelled and how differently it was read at a distance. Guilt and innocence were bitterly contested for twelve years. The chapter keeps to the dated record: what each court ruled, what each witness claimed, and the fact that on 12 July 1906 France's highest court annulled the last conviction and declared that nothing of the accusation remained.

intro: On 20 November 1945, in a courtroom rebuilt inside Nuremberg's Palace of Justice, twenty-one leaders of the defeated German state sat in two rows of a wooden dock while judges from the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and France heard the case against them. Nothing quite like it had been tried before: the victors had agreed in London on 8 August to put an enemy government on trial under a written charter, for planning aggressive war, for war crimes, and for a new category, crimes against humanity. The trial ran for almost a year. The judgment was read on 30 September and 1 October 1946; ten men were hanged in the prison gymnasium in the early hours of 16 October, and Hermann Göring escaped the rope by poison the evening before. The court's own record is unusually full. Every word spoken was interpreted at once into four languages through headphones, taken down by stenographers and printed in the 42 volumes of the official 'Blue Series'. It is the main source here, and it carries the voices that no diary could: the defendants' pleas and testimony, the prosecutors' speeches, the cross-examinations, and witnesses ranging from an Auschwitz survivor, Marie-Claude Vaillant-Couturier, to the former Auschwitz commandant, Rudolf Höss. Atrocity evidence is reported here as the court recorded it, with figures and without detail. Around the record stand the private and public writers. Thomas Dodd, the American trial counsel, wrote home to his wife every few days, and his letters give the trial's ordinary texture: staff quarrels, slow colleagues, homesickness, a week on the Riviera while the judges deliberated. David Maxwell Fyfe, who led the British in court, wrote to his wife too, though his letters are known here only through quotation. The prison psychologist G. M. Gilbert kept notes of his daily conversations with the defendants, published in 1947 as Nuremberg Diary: a real diary, but one written up for print by a man who made no secret of his views. Airey Neave, who served the indictment, set down his memories thirty years later. The press supplied the rest. Janet Flanner's New Yorker 'Letters' of March 1946 judged that Göring had outplayed Jackson, and her editor sent Rebecca West to replace her; West's long reports caught the tedium of the court as sharply as the faces in the dock. Kingsbury Smith of the International News Service, chosen by lot, wrote the account of the executions that most of the world read. Some of these sources are dated diaries or letters, many are dated documents of the court, and some are reportage or later recollection; each is labelled for what it is. Read together, they disagree. Dodd thought Jackson's cross-examination of Göring went well; Maxwell Fyfe and most reporters did not. Göring treated the trial as victors' justice; Speer accepted a general share of responsibility; Höss described his own work in figures. The judgment itself split: the Soviet judge dissented from the three acquittals. Where the court ruled, this chapter reports the ruling; it adds no verdict of its own on the questions the trial still raises about law made by victors.

intro: On 3 May 1946, eight months after the surrender, twenty-eight former leaders of Japan were brought into the auditorium of the old Army Ministry on Ichigaya Heights in Tokyo, refitted with floodlights, interpreters' booths and a long bench for eleven judges from eleven nations. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East had been created on 19 January 1946 by an order of General MacArthur, and it would sit until 12 November 1948. Seven of the accused were hanged at Sugamo Prison in the first hour of 23 December 1948. The honest record of this trial is mostly not diaries. It is the court's own transcript, exhibits and judgment; the telegrams and statements of the occupying power; the affidavits and testimony of the accused; and the separate opinions of judges who could not agree. Two dated private diaries stand beside them: the Chinese judge Mei Ruao's notes from his hotel room in the spring of 1946, and the diplomat Shigemitsu Mamoru's prison diary from Sugamo. A third diary, Kido Kōichi's daily record of court politics from 1930 to 1945, entered the trial as the prosecution's key exhibit. The eyes are chosen to give the prosecution, the defence and the bench equal weight. Keenan presented the accused as planners of aggressive war; Kiyose and the American counsel Blakeney argued that the charges were law made after the fact, and set Hiroshima beside Pearl Harbor. Tōjō defended the war as self-defence while shielding the Emperor. On the last day the court split five ways: a majority that convicted all twenty-five survivors, Pal of India who would have acquitted them all, Röling of the Netherlands who dissented in both directions, Bernard of France who objected to how the judgment was reached, and Jaranilla of the Philippines, a survivor of Bataan, who thought the sentences too light. This chapter reports those positions and adds no verdict of its own. One absence shapes everything: the Emperor. MacArthur's January 1946 telegram advising against an indictment, Keenan's cross-examination of Tōjō in January 1948, Bernard's dissent and Webb's separate opinion all circle the man who was never charged. The evidence of atrocity, from Nanjing to the prisoner-of-war camps, is reported here as the court recorded it, with its scale and the witnesses' names, and without detail. Copyright limits what can be quoted. Short phrases appear only from US-government publications such as Foreign Relations of the United States; the transcript, the judgment, the opinions and all diaries and memoirs are given as digests in plain words. Where a date comes from standard accounts rather than a document seen, the entry is marked approximate.
